A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of

BACKGROUND: The timing of antihypertensive drugs administration is controversial. The aim was to compare the efficacy of
dosing of antihypertensive drugs in the morning versus evening.
METHODS: A PubMed, EMBASE, and clinicaltrials.gov databases search for randomized clinical trials of antihypertensive
therapies where patients were randomized to morning versus evening dosing. The outcomes were ambulatory blood pressure
(BP) parameters (day-time, night-time, and 24/48-hour systolic blood pressure [SBP] and diastolic blood pressure [DBP])
and cardiovascular outcomes.

24/48-hour SBP (mean difference [MD]=1.41 mm Hg; [95% CI, 0.48–2.34]), DBP (MD=0.60 mm Hg [95% CI, 0.12–

reduction in day-time SBP (MD=0.94 mm Hg [95% CI, 0.01–1.87]), and DBP (MD=0.87 mm Hg [95% CI, 0.10–1.63]), and
numerically lower cardiovascular events compared with morning dosing. However,

accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic
Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines.38 This analysis was

a trial level meta-analysis of published clinical trial data. The
protocol of this meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO
(CRD42022333583). The data that support the findings of
this study are available from the corresponding author upon
reasonable request.
Data (collection sheets) would be made available at a rea-
sonable request.

A time limited search until August 26, 2022 was conducted
using PubMed and EMBASE databases. The following Medical
Education Subject Headings were used for this search: “chrono-
therapy,” “conventional therapy,” “antihypertensives,” “hyperten-
sion,” “morning dose,” “evening dose,” “adverse cardiovascular
events,” “night time b

The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials

[DBP]) and clinical outcomes. Studies with a placebo com-
parison arm (eg, morning versus placebo and evening versus
placebo) or without a comparison arm, observational studies,
editorials, letters, and review articles were excluded.
We used PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison,
and Outcome) criteria for study selection.39 Population of
interest: hypertensive patients who were enrolled in anti-
hypertensive trials of morning versus evening dosing; inter-
vention: antihypertensive drug evening dosing; comparison:
antihypertensive drug morning dosing; outcomes: reduction
in ambulatory BP.

What Is New?
This systematic review and meta-analysis of 72 ran-
domized controlled trials evaluated the effect of anti-
hypertensive drugs morning versus evening dosing
and showed significant reduction of ambulatory blood
pressure (BP) and numerically lower risk of major
adverse cardiac event, cardiovascular mortality, all-
cause mortality, and heart failure in patients random-

adverse cardiac event, cardiovascular mortality, all-
cause mortality, and heart failure in patients random-
ized to evening dosing when compared with morning.
When controversial single-center data by Hermida et
al were omitted, evening dosing of antihypertensive
drugs significantly reduced night-time ambulatory BP
but had no effect on other ambulatory BP parameters
and on cardiovascular outcomes.
What Is Relevant?
BP reduction with antihypertensive agents reduces
cardiovascular events. However, the optimal timing of
medication administration is unknown. The trials con-
ducted on the efficacy of antihypertensive drugs morn-
ing versus evening dosing were small-scale and had
heterogeneous outcomes. Particularly, multiple data
from a single center have suggested improved 24/48-
hour BP control and outcome with evening dosing.
Evening dosing of antihypertensive drugs significantly
reduce night-time BP when compared with morning
dosing but has no certain effect on other ambulatory
BP parameters and on cardiovascular outcomes, but
results were largely driven by trials conducted by Her-
mida and colleagues.
Clinical/Pathophysiological Implications?
Unless the intention is to specifically lower nighttime
BP, antihypertensive drugs should be taken at a time
of day that is convenient, optimizes adherence and
minimizes undesirable effects.

Study Outcomes
The efficacy outcomes were reduction in ambulatory SBP and
DBP at day-time, night-time, and 24/48-hour BP in mm Hg.
Ambulatory 24/48-hour BP was based on either 24- or
48-hour BP measurements. Clinical outcomes were major
adverse cardiac event (MACE; defined as a composite of
angina, myocardial infarction, heart failure, vascular interven-
tions, stroke, cardiovascular and all-cause mortality), all-cause
mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and heart failure.
Data Analysis
Data Extraction and Quality Assessment
The studies were screened by 2 independent authors (M.H.M.
and S.B.). Nonrelevant studies were excluded based on title fol-
lowed by abstract. Full text studies were then screened for final
selection on basis of above-mentioned, prespecified inclusion
criteria. Two reviewers (M.H.M. and S.B.) independently reviewed
the literature, extracted and entered data. Discrepancies were
resolved by discussion. Two authors independently appraised
the methodological quality of included trials using the Cochrane
Risk of Bias Tool which assessed selection, allocation, perfor-
mance, detection, attrition, and reporting bias (Table S1).40

studies was assessed using I2 statistic.42 I2 value <25%, 25% to

This meta-analysis of 72 RCTs evaluating the effect
of antihypertensive drugs morning versus evening dos-
ing showed significant reduction of ambulatory BP,
and numerically lower risk of cardiovascular events in

clinical outcomes.

Study Limitations
The results of this analysis should be interpreted consider-
ing certain limitations. First, our analysis consisted mainly
of small-scale RCTs in specific geographic areas so the
extent of generalizability and trends in different popula-
tions is unknown. Second, adherence with antihypertensive
drugs was not reported in most of these trials. Third, not all
commercially available antihypertensive drugs were repre-
sented in this meta-analysis. Fourthly, there was variability in
drug administration between trials with few trials designed
to give all of the antihypertensive medications in the eve-
ning while in others only a few antihypertensive medications
were given in the evening. Finally, there is a potential for
overlap of patients in different Hermida trials, which could
artificially increase the benefits of evening dose.

Timing of Antihypertensive Dosing and Efficacy

Perspectives
The trials conducted on the efficacy of antihypertensive
drugs morning versus evening dosing were small-scale
and had heterogeneous outcomes. Particularly, multiple
data from a single center have suggested improved
24/48-hour BP control and outcome with evening
dosing. A time limited search until May 28, 2022 was
conducted using PubMed, EMBASE, and clinicaltrials.
gov databases for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of
antihypertensive drug therapies where patients were
randomized to morning versus evening dosing. This sys-
tematic review and meta-analysis of 72 RCTs evaluates
the effect of antihypertensive drugs morning versus eve-
ning dosing, which showed that evening dosing of anti-
hypertensive drugs significantly reduced ambulatory BP
parameters and lowered cardiovascular events but the
effect was mainly driven by trials by Hermida et al. Unless
the intention is to specifically lower night-time BP, anti-
hypertensive drugs should be taken at a time of day that
is convenient, optimizes adherence, and minimizes unde-
sirable effects.
